The three output terminals make sense as a hallway with two doors:

Which relay module should you buy?

The 1-channel and 2-channel relay modules below are the same circuit — same red PCB, screw terminals, opto-coupler, indicator LEDs and trigger-select jumper — so pick by how many loads you switch.

What is the HIGH/LOW trigger jumper for?

The HIGH/LOW trigger jumper — a small black cap on a three-pin header marked H and L — decides which logic level pulls the relay in. In the L position the board is low-level triggered: the relay energises when IN is pulled LOW ; in the H position it energises when IN is driven HIGH.

...

Close-up cartoon of the high low level trigger select jumper on a red relay module PCB in its two positions The trigger-select jumper: same board, two personalities. Check which pair the cap sits on before trusting any sketch.

How do you wire a relay module to an Arduino Uno?

The relay module pinout is six screw positions: DC+, DC− and IN on the control side, NO, COM and NC on the output side — screw terminals on both edges, not header pins. IN only drives the opto-coupler’s LED — a 15–20mA load per channel — while the coil’s ~71mA comes from DC+; an Uno GPIO is only rated for 20mA per pin , which is why the coil never hangs off a pin.

The ShillehTek 1-Channel 5V Relay Module lets an Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi Pico switch a single high-voltage or high-current load with a low-voltage logic signal. The on-board SRD-05VDC-SL-C relay can switch up to 10A at 250VAC or 10A at 30VDC, making it suitable for controlling lamps, fans, motors, solenoids, water pumps, and AC mains appliances from a microcontroller.
The module is opto-coupled and uses an active-LOW input — pull the IN pin LOW to energize the relay coil and close the contacts. A red LED indicates relay state and a green LED indicates power. Three screw terminals (NO, COM, NC) provide both Normally Open and Normally Closed switching options, so you can wire it as either a "switch ON" or "switch OFF" device for your load.
This 5V variant is the most beginner-friendly relay because it can be powered directly from the 5V rail of an Arduino UNO, Raspberry Pi, or Pico — no external power supply required for the module itself.

results.title: 5V Relay Module (SRD-05VDC-SL-C): Pinout, Wiring & Specs | Tinkered
excerpts:
A single-channel 5V relay module (SONGLE SRD-05VDC-SL-C) that lets a microcontroller switch a high-power AC or DC load through isolated SPDT contacts rated 10A at 250VAC / 30VDC.

...

At its heart is a SONGLE SRD-05VDC-SL-C relay: a 5V coil that, when energized, moves an internal armature to physically open and close a set of contacts. Because those contacts are mechanically and electrically isolated from the coil, the Arduino side stays safely separated from whatever you are switching.
The relay is SPDT (single pole, double throw, also called 1 Form C), so it exposes three switched terminals: COM (common), NO (normally open), and NC (normally closed). With the coil off, COM connects to NC; energize the coil and COM switches over to NO. The bare coil draws roughly 70mA at 5V, far more than a GPIO pin can source, so the module adds a driver transistor, an indicator LED, and a flyback diode across the coil. You connect only VCC, GND, and the logic-level IN pin to your controller.
The contacts are rated for 10A at 250VAC or 10A at 30VDC, which covers most lamps, pumps, fans, and small appliances.

...

* Give the module a steady 5V on VCC and GND. The energized coil pulls roughly 70mA, so let the onboard transistor drive it and connect only the IN pin to your microcontroller, never the coil directly.
* Share a common ground between the module and the controller. Without it the IN signal has no reference and switching becomes unreliable.
* IN is a logic-level digital input. On many single-channel boards the trigger is active-LOW (a LOW output energizes the relay), so verify your board's polarity before writing the sketch.
* The COM, NO, and NC contacts are isolated from the coil. Wire the load in series through COM and NO (or NC) using its own supply, and never route mains or high load current through the Arduino or a breadboard.
* Keep contact current and voltage well under the 10A / 250VAC / 30VDC rating. For inductive loads such as motors or solenoids, add an RC snubber across AC contacts or a flyback diode across a DC load to reduce arcing and extend contact life.

The KY-019 5V Relay Module — also sold as the **CW-019** , HW-482, and Keyes SR1Y — is a single-channel relay breakout board that lets an Arduino switch high-voltage AC or DC loads with a 5V digital signal. Common in Arduino starter kits, it features a Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C relay with Normally Open (NO) and Normally Closed (NC) contacts and an LED indicator for signal state.

Unlike the blue optocoupler relay boards that are active-LOW, the KY-019 is **active-HIGH** — the relay energizes when the signal pin is driven HIGH.

...

Compatible with Arduino, Raspberry Pi, and ESP32 (the signal pin accepts 3.3V logic for triggering; the relay coil still requires 5V on VCC).

...

The KY-019 consists of a Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C relay, an NPN transistor driver, a signal LED, and a 1N4007 flyback diode to suppress coil back-EMF. The DC side has three pins (S, +, −); the AC side has three contacts (NC, COM, NO).

## KY-019 Pinout

|Label |Function |
| --- | --- |
|**S** |Signal — active-HIGH: relay and indicator LED turn on when HIGH (3.3–5 V) |
|**\+** |VCC — 5 V supply for the relay coil and onboard circuitry |
|**−** |GND — ground |
|**NC** |Normally Closed — connected to COM when the relay is _off_ |
|**COM** |Common — the AC/DC load’s switching terminal |
|**NO** |Normally Open — connected to COM when the relay is _on_ |

The KY-019 uses **active-HIGH logic** : pulling the **S pin HIGH** energises the coil and switches **COM** from **NC** to **NO** . The indicator LED turns on at the same time. **CW-019** and **HW-482** clones follow the same pinout and active-HIGH behaviour. **COM** is the middle terminal on the relay’s AC/DC side.

## How the KY-019 Works

The KY-019 is an electrically operated switch. When the Arduino pulls the **S pin HIGH** , current flows through an **NPN transistor** on the board, energising the **relay coil** (a Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C).

...
